extracted.intended_audience: Heads of executive agencies, regulatory analysts, and agency staff preparing regulatory analyses for Federal rulemakings
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing regulatory analyses (benefit-cost and cost-effectiveness) to support economically significant and other major Federal rulemakings, including required specialized analyses and accounting statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key elements of a regulatory analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A good regulatory analysis should include the following three basic elements: (1) a statement of the need for the proposed action, (2) an examination of alternative approaches, and (3) an evaluation of the benefits and costs—quantitative and qualitative—of the proposed action and the main alternatives identified by the analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these three elements as the organizing framework for analyses; ensure each element is addressed explicitly and linked to the rest of the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain linkage from actions to expected benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain how the actions required by the rule are linked to the expected benefits (e.g., indicate how additional safety equipment will reduce safety risks). A similar analysis should be done for each of the alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make causal chains explicit so readers can see how regulatory requirements produce benefits; do this for each alternative examined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify a clear baseline
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify a baseline. Benefits and costs are defined in comparison with a clearly stated alternative. This normally will be a 'no action' baseline: what the world will be like if the proposed rule is not adopted. Comparisons to a 'next best' alternative are also especially useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State baseline assumptions explicitly; where useful, present both no-action and next-best baselines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify undesirable side-effects and ancillary benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the expected undesirable side-effects and ancillary benefits of the proposed regulatory action and the alternatives. These should be added to the direct benefits and costs as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List ancillary effects and consider including them in quantitative or qualitative comparisons of alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantified and non-quantified benefits and costs
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete regulatory analysis includes a discussion of non-quantified as well as quantified benefits and costs. When there are important non-monetary values at stake, identify them so policymakers can compare them with monetary benefits and costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When monetization is infeasible, clearly describe non-quantified factors and their likely importance; do not ignore important non-monetary outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold (break-even) analysis for non-quantified effects
rubrics_metrics.description: If non-quantified benefits and costs are likely to be important, carry out a 'threshold' analysis to evaluate their significance. Threshold or 'break-even' analysis answers: 'How small could the value of the non-quantified benefits be (or how large would the value of the non-quantified costs need to be) before the rule would yield zero net benefits?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide break-even calculations to show how large non-monetized values would need to be to change policy conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek consultation and stakeholder input
rubrics_metrics.description: As you design, execute, and write your regulatory analysis, seek out the opinions of those who will be affected by the regulation as well as those with special knowledge or insight. Consultation can ensure the analysis addresses relevant issues and obtains pertinent data; early consultation is especially helpful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document consultation efforts and incorporate findings; do not limit consultation to the final stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use professional judgment and tailor emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: You cannot conduct a good regulatory analysis according to a formula. Conducting high-quality analysis requires competent professional judgment. Different regulations may call for different emphases depending on nature, complexity, and sensitivity of estimates to assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why particular emphases or methods were chosen based on the rule's context; justify departures from standard approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: A good analysis is transparent. It should be possible for a qualified third party to see clearly how estimates and conclusions were derived. State assumptions (time horizon, discount rates), provide sensitivity analysis, specific references to sources, appendices with models, and results of formal uncertainty analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include an executive summary and standardized accounting statement; provide appendices and full documentation sufficient for independent review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate necessity of Federal regulatory action
rubrics_metrics.description: Before recommending Federal regulatory action, an agency must demonstrate the proposed action is necessary. Describe the specific authority, extent of discretion, and the regulatory instruments considered. Identify the problem and assess its significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain whether the action addresses a significant market failure or another compelling public need and present qualitative and, where feasible, quantitative evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe market failure or other social purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain whether the action is intended to address a market failure (externality, market power, inadequate/asymmetric information) or other purposes (improve government functioning, redistribute, prohibit discrimination, protect privacy). Describe failures qualitatively and, where feasible, quantitatively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document the nature of the failure and show that government intervention is likely to do more good than harm; for information-processing problems, provide careful documentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider non-federal alternatives and proper government level
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider alternatives to Federal regulation (antitrust, litigation, administrative compensation) and possibility of State or local regulation. Examine the proper extent of State and local discretion and potential for harmonization or reducing duplicative rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess tradeoffs between national uniformity and benefits of local experimentation; consider international harmonization and non-tariff barrier effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption against certain economic regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a presumption against certain types of regulatory action. Particularly demanding burden of proof is required for price controls in competitive markets; production/sales quotas; mandatory uniform quality standards if voluntary measures suffice; and controls on entry into employment or production except where indispensable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid regulations that unnecessarily impede market efficiency; provide strong justification when proposing these types of measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider a range of alternative regulatory approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Once Federal action is appropriate, consider alternative approaches including different statutory choices, compliance dates, enforcement methods, degrees of stringency, different requirements by firm size, and different requirements by geographic region.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eliminate some alternatives via preliminary analysis but evaluate a manageable set in detail; justify selection of alternatives for detailed comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate different compliance dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider alternative compliance dates, since timing may affect net benefits. Delays may reduce benefits or reduce costs if firms need lead time to comply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how compliance timing affects both benefits and costs and consider lead times to minimize overall costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate different enforcement methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider enforcement and compliance alternatives (on-site inspections, periodic reporting, penalties, random or parametric monitoring) and identify the most appropriate enforcement framework given benefits and costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess monitoring costs and effectiveness; consider less costly methods that are nearly as effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider different degrees of stringency
rubrics_metrics.description: Study alternative levels of stringency to understand how benefits and costs—and their distribution—change. Generally both benefits and costs increase with stringency, but marginal patterns differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze incremental effects of moving to more stringent options and examine distributional consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider different requirements by firm size
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider setting different requirements for large and small firms based on estimated differences in compliance costs or expected benefits. Remember significant impacts on many small entities trigger Regulatory Flexibility Act requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid imposing disproportionate burdens on small entities without justification and consult Chief Counsel for Advocacy when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider different regional requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: When benefits or costs vary significantly across regions, consider setting different regional requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether regional tailoring improves net benefits while noting potential costs from fragmented regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer performance standards over design standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Performance standards express outcomes rather than prescribing means; they generally provide regulated parties flexibility to achieve objectives in a cost-effective way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for cost savings from flexibility and costs of monitoring compliance when choosing between performance and design standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider market-oriented approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Explore market-oriented alternatives using economic incentives (fees, penalties, subsidies, marketable permits/offsets, changes in liability or property rights, bonds/insurance/warranties). These can reduce costs or achieve earlier or greater benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider ABT (averaging, banking, trading) where appropriate, while guarding against unacceptable local outcomes (e.g., hot spots).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider informational measures before regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: If failure arises from inadequate or asymmetric information, informational remedies (standardized testing/rating, mandatory disclosure, government provision of information) may be preferred to regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate costs (gathering, communicating info, displaced info, misinterpretation) and consider least-intrusive informational alternatives sufficient to meet objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Benefit-Cost Analysis where feasible
rubrics_metrics.description: BCA expresses both benefits and costs in monetary units to evaluate alternative regulatory choices and identify the alternative that maximizes net benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure incremental benefits and costs of successively more stringent alternatives; avoid using benefit-cost ratios alone as indicators of net benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Cost-Effectiveness Analysis when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: CEA is appropriate when primary benefits are improved public health and safety and a valid effectiveness measure can be developed, or when some benefits cannot be monetized but CEA can compare options with the same primary outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer final outcome measures (lives saved, life-years) over intermediate outputs; present incremental CEA and beware of average ratios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do both BCA and CEA for many major rulemakings
rubrics_metrics.description: A major rulemaking should be supported by both BCA and CEA wherever possible. Specifically, prepare a CEA for major health and safety rulemakings where a valid effectiveness measure exists, and perform a BCA for major health and safety rulemakings to the extent valid monetary values can be assigned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When primary benefits cannot all be monetized, do both analyses and present qualitative discussions where no quantified info exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure incremental rather than average comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: By measuring incremental benefits and costs of successively more stringent regulatory alternatives, you can identify the alternative that maximizes net benefits. The ratio of benefits to costs is not a meaningful indicator of net benefits and should not be used for that purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on incremental net benefits and incremental cost-effectiveness ratios; eliminate dominated alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct cost and effectiveness measures carefully in CEA
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure numerator (net costs) includes all relevant public and private costs minus cost savings; avoid double-counting. Choose effectiveness measures that reflect final outcomes and capture variability in quality of units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain choice of effectiveness measure and adjust when multiple beneficial outcomes must be integrated or weighted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness metrics for public health and safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Use measures such as lives saved, life-years saved, 'equivalent lives' (ELs), or quality-adjusted life years (QALYs); integrated measures account for morbidity as well as mortality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of assumptions (e.g., QALY assumptions) and consider using at least one integrated measure when impacts on mortality and morbidity are significant; adjust for fairness across population segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of risk and uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide expected-value estimates and distributions where available. Use sensitivity analyses to reveal whether results are sensitive to plausible changes in assumptions and numeric inputs. Where only bounds are provided, use 95 and 5 percent bounds if possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be transparent about uncertainty; if alternative plausible assumptions change conclusions, analyze assumptions further and document rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume risk neutrality generally
rubrics_metrics.description: Although not always the case, assume 'risk neutrality' in analysis in general. If adopting different assumptions on risk preference, explain reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State risk-preference assumptions explicitly and test alternatives in sensitivity analysis if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make alternative assumptions explicit and test sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: If estimates depend heavily on certain assumptions, make them explicit and carry out sensitivity analyses using plausible alternatives. If net benefits change sign or rankings change, conduct further analysis to determine appropriate assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report alternative scenarios and explain the choice of the preferred assumption set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialized analyses required by statute or EO
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of statutory and Executive Order analytic requirements, including Regulatory Flexibility Act (small entities), Unfunded Mandates Act, Paperwork Reduction Act, Information Quality Guidelines, NEPA, EO 13045 (children), and EO 13211 (energy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform and document these specialized analyses when the rule meets statutory/EO triggers and follow the specific procedures and thresholds set by the statutes and orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Flexibility Act analysis for small entities
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the RFA (5 U.S.C. chapter 6), prepare proposed and final regulatory flexibility analyses if the rule could 'have a significant impact on a substantial number of small entities.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult agency guidelines and the SBA Chief Counsel for Advocacy; consider posting the RFA online and follow SBREFA requirements when applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unfunded Mandates Act statement for large aggregate expenditures
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Unfunded Mandates Act (2 U.S.C. 1532), prepare a written statement about benefits and costs prior to issuing a proposed or final rule that may result in aggregate expenditures of $100,000,000 or more in any one year (adjusted annually).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate Unfunded Mandates analysis with Executive Order 12866 analyses to the extent possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paperwork Reduction Act compliance for information collections
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the rule will create any additional information collection, paperwork or recordkeeping burdens. OMB approval is required for collections on 10 or more persons and an OMB control number is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justify practical utility of information; work with agency CIO and OMB to obtain necessary approvals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information Quality Guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Information Quality Law and OMB/agency guidelines, data and analysis used to support rules must meet quality performance goals for information disseminated by agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow agency and OMB information quality standards and document data provenance and quality assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: NEPA compliance and environmental documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: NEPA and related statutes require agencies to consider environmental impacts of decisions, including rulemakings. An environmental impact statement must be prepared for 'major Federal actions significantly affecting the quality of the human environment.' NEPA documentation must be completed before issuing a final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow CEQ regulations and guidance and coordinate NEPA requirements with rulemaking schedule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address impacts on children (EO 13045)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under EO 13045, agencies must, to the extent permitted by law and appropriate, address disproportionate risks to children from environmental health and safety risks. For economically significant rules likely to affect children, provide OMB/OIRA an evaluation and explanation of why the planned regulation is preferable to other feasible alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess and document potential disproportionate child impacts and alternative measures considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of Energy Effects for significant energy actions (EO 13211)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under EO 13211, prepare and submit to OMB a Statement of Energy Effects for significant energy actions, including detailed statements of adverse effects on energy supply, distribution, or use, and publish the statement or summary in the NPRM and final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow OMB Memorandum 01-27 for implementing EO 13211 and include energy impacts in the regulatory record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting statement and standardized reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide an accounting statement with tables reporting benefit and cost estimates for each major final rule. Report estimates in three categories: monetized; quantified but not monetized; and qualitative but not quantified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use suggested formats and avoid double-counting; include footnotes for documentation and warnings as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorize benefits and costs and avoid double-counting
rubrics_metrics.description: Report benefits and costs in mutually exclusive and exhaustive categories and avoid double-counting effects (e.g., the same welfare change expressed in multiple ways).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use consistent categories and check for double-counting when assembling estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of benefits and costs over time and discounting
rubrics_metrics.description: Present undiscounted streams of benefit and cost estimates for each year of the analytic time horizon and annualized benefits and costs using real discount rates of 3 and 7 percent. Report all monetized effects in 2001 dollars and convert other years using the GDP deflator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin streams in the year effects start; include both undiscounted and annualized estimates and state discounting assumptions explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision and rounding of estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported estimates should reflect feasible precision in analysis. For example, $220 million implies rounding to the nearest $10 million (precision +/- $5 million); $222 million implies rounding to the nearest $1 million (precision +/- $0.5 million).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Round estimates consistently and in a manner that reflects true precision; document rounding conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report expected-values and distributions for uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide expected-value estimates as well as distributions where such information exists. When only upper and lower bounds are provided, use 95 and 5 percent confidence bounds if possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make distributions available on request; where uncertainty importantly affects inferences, describe benefits/costs under plausible alternative assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate reporting of transfers
rubrics_metrics.description: Report transfers separately and avoid misclassifying transfer payments as benefits or costs. Distinguish transfers caused by Federal budget actions from transfers between non-governmental parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as many categories as necessary to describe redistributive effects and identify transfers that also have efficiency effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify distributional impacts: state, local, tribal, small business, wages, growth
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify portions of benefits, costs, and transfers received by State, local, and tribal governments. To the extent feasible, identify effects on small businesses, wages, and economic growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where feasible, quantify distributional effects and report them alongside aggregate estimates; note that rules with annual costs < $1 billion are likely to have minimal effect on economic growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid double-counting across measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid double-counting effects across monetized and non-monetized categories or within cost-effectiveness ratios (e.g., do not count life-extension monetized value in costs if life-years are used as effectiveness measure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check numerator and denominator of ratios for overlapping measures and adjust calculations accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Round out analysis with executive summary
rubrics_metrics.description: Include an executive summary, including a standardized accounting statement, so readers can quickly evaluate benefit and cost estimates and qualitative factors for each alternative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the executive summary self-contained with the principal findings, key assumptions, and a standardized accounting table.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use integrated measures carefully and note assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrated effectiveness measures (e.g., QALYs, ELs) account for morbidity and mortality but require restrictive assumptions (e.g., assumptions about preference independence). If assumptions are questionable, note potential differences versus willingness-to-pay measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using integrated measures, disclose restrictive assumptions and consider providing alternative measures or monetary valuations for comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use incremental cost-effectiveness and dominance concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: When constructing and comparing incremental cost-effectiveness ratios, determine whether alternatives are mutually exclusive or combinable; eliminate inferior alternatives identified by principles of strong and weak dominance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present incremental comparisons relative to the next less-stringent alternative and explain why dominated options are excluded.
